text.p: Convicted murderer Coleman Wayne Gray was put to death by lethal injection on Wednesday for murdering a grocery store manager nearly 12 years ago. The procedure took about six minutes.

Gray, 39, was convicted of the May 1985 murder of grocery store manager Richard McClelland. His case had wound its way through the legal system for more than 11 years with countless hearings and appeals to state and federal courts. The final ruling of the Supreme Court came only 10 minutes before the execution.

An all-white jury convicted Gray, who was black, of robbing and abducting McClelland, a white, and shooting him six times in the back of the head despite his pleas for mercy. He was found guilty largely on the testimony of his accomplice, Melvin Tucker, but Gray insisted that Tucker was the trigger man.

Gray, looking scared and shaking, was led into the execution chamber at 8:50 p.m. by eight uniformed guards. He was quickly brought to a gurney in the centre of the room where one guard lifted up his legs and another pushed him down by the shoulders.

Guards working quickly then strapped him down at the ankles, thighs, chest and attached cross straps from his shoulders to his waist as Gray looked around the room, his lips fluttering. It took two minutes for technicians to stretch out each arm and attach intravenous drips. His hands were bandaged down.
Gray was asked if he had any last words. "I have no last statement," he said.

The execution staff then began to inject the deadly chemicals. For two minutes Gray's chest heaved violently, before his breathing subsided and then stopped. Just before death was pronounced, his chest twitched twice.

Gray's last day was a rush of legal activity as his lawyer rushed about in a futile attempt to halt the execution. The U.S. Supreme Court, Gov. George Allen and a U.S. District Court all refused to intervene.
Gray's mother and sister visited him but were required to leave during the afternoon. Gray ate his last meal of fried chicken, french fries and an apple.

Ron Angelone, director of the Virginia Department of Corrections, told Reuters lethal injection was the preferred method of execution partly because it was emotionally easier on the corrections officers carrying out the execution.
"It makes it a lot easier for them to deal with emotionally," he said.
"The process does not aim to dehumanize the person being executed, but it's not designed to provide them with dignity either. It's done without emotion," he said.
